summary: Specifies the protocol an IPv6 router uses to discover which neighboring nodes want to receive multicast packets, and which multicast addresses they are interested in. It is the IPv6 counterpart of IGMP. It is a standards-track protocol at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: A teacher asks who wants to hear each announcement and writes down the hands that go up. MLD is how a router asks that question on a network.

questions: how does ipv6 multicast membership work
how does mld differ from igmp
subtitle: How an IPv6 router learns which multicast addresses have listeners on each attached link.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 router must know which multicast addresses have interested receivers on each directly attached link, so it can deliver multicast packets only where they are wanted.
tldr.mechanism: A Querier router periodically sends Queries; listeners answer with Reports after a random delay, and send a Done message when they stop listening. The router keeps a timer per address and tells its multicast routing protocol when listeners appear or vanish.
tldr.outcome: MLD is a Proposed Standard derived from IGMPv2, and it has been updated by RFC 3590, RFC 3810 and RFC 9777.

today: RFC 2710 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 3590, RFC 3810 and RFC 9777. It is not marked as obsoleted.

sections.title: Purpose of MLD
sections.content:
Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) lets each IPv6 router discover multicast listeners, meaning nodes that want to receive multicast packets, on its directly attached links, and learn which multicast addresses they care about. The router gives this to its multicast routing protocol so packets reach every link with interested receivers.

MLD is derived from version 2 of IPv4's IGMP (IGMPv2). The notable difference is that it uses ICMPv6 message types (IP protocol 58) rather than IGMP message types (IP protocol 2).

MLD is asymmetric: listeners and routers behave differently. A router that is itself listening to an address performs both parts, including answering its own messages. A router with several interfaces to the same link needs to run the router part on only one, while listeners must run the listener part on every interface where reception was requested.
sections.eli5: A router wants to know which rooms have someone who wants to hear the radio, so it only plays the radio in those rooms.

sections.title: MLD Message Format
sections.content:
MLD messages are a subset of ICMPv6, identified by a Next Header value of 58. Every message is sent with a link-local IPv6 source address, a Hop Limit of 1, and an IPv6 Router Alert option in a Hop-by-Hop Options header. The Router Alert makes routers examine messages sent to multicast addresses they have no interest in.

There are three types: Query (decimal 130), Report (131) and Done (132). A Query is either a General Query, with a Multicast Address of zero, or a Multicast-Address-Specific Query naming one address. The Maximum Response Delay is in milliseconds and matters only in Queries. The Code and Reserved fields are zero and ignored on receipt.

A message is 24 octets. Implementations MUST NOT send longer messages and MUST ignore anything past the first 24 octets of a received one, though the checksum MUST cover the entire message.
sections.eli5: There are only three kinds of notes: a question asking who is listening, an answer saying I am, and a goodbye saying I stopped.

sections.title: How Queries, Reports and Done Work
sections.content:
Per link, a router is either Querier or Non-Querier. All routers start as Querier. If a router hears a Query from a numerically lower source address, it MUST become a Non-Querier. After the Other Querier Present Interval passes without such a Query, it becomes Querier again. The Querier sends a General Query every Query Interval to the all-nodes address FF02::1, and on startup SHOULD send several closely spaced ones.

When a node hears a General Query, it starts a timer for each multicast address it listens to, with a random value up to the Maximum Response Delay. It excludes the all-nodes address and addresses of scope 0 or 1. When a timer expires the node sends a Report to the address being reported. If it hears another node's Report for the same address first, it stops its timer and stays silent, which suppresses duplicate Reports.

The router keeps a list of addresses with listeners on each link, each with a timer reset by every Report. It does not need to know who or how many the listeners are. If a timer expires, the address is removed and the routing component is told.

A node that starts listening sends an unsolicited Report at once and SHOULD repeat it after short delays. A node that stops listening SHOULD send a Done message to the all-routers address FF02::2. On a Done, the Querier sends Multicast-Address-Specific Queries, and if no Report arrives the address is dropped. Non-Queriers MUST ignore Done messages.
sections.eli5: The teacher asks who wants to hear about dinosaurs. Kids wait a random moment, and if someone else already raised a hand, the rest stay quiet. When the last kid loses interest, the teacher asks once more before crossing dinosaurs off the list.

sections.title: Node and Router State Machines
sections.content:
For each multicast address on each interface, a node is in one of three states: Non-Listener, Delaying Listener (timer running) or Idle Listener (no timer). The five events are start listening, stop listening, query received, report received and timer expired. A Query or Report is valid only if it has a link-local source address, is at least 24 octets long and has a correct checksum. The all-nodes address FF02::1 is a special case: the node stays in Idle Listener and never sends a Report or Done for it.

A router has per-link Querier and Non-Querier states, and per-address states: No Listeners Present, Listeners Present and Checking Listeners. A router in Checking Listeners continues the Querier behavior until it hears a Report or its timer expires, even if it has become a Non-Querier in the meantime.
sections.eli5: Each kid is either not interested, waiting to answer, or has already answered. The teacher keeps a list of which topics still have interested kids.

sections.title: Timers and Default Values
sections.content:
Most timers are configurable, but non-default settings MUST be consistent among all routers on a link. The Robustness Variable (default 2) tunes for expected packet loss and MUST NOT be zero and SHOULD NOT be one. The Query Interval defaults to 125 seconds and the Query Response Interval to 10000 milliseconds, which must be less than the Query Interval.

The Multicast Listener Interval, after which a router decides an address has no listeners, MUST be the Robustness Variable times the Query Interval plus one Query Response Interval. The Other Querier Present Interval is the Robustness Variable times the Query Interval plus half of one Query Response Interval. The Last Listener Query Interval defaults to 1000 milliseconds and can be lowered to cut leave latency. The Unsolicited Report Interval defaults to 10 seconds.
sections.eli5: These are the stopwatch settings: how often the teacher asks, how long kids may take to answer, and how long to wait before deciding nobody cares.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC examines a forged message of each type. Because nodes check that the source address is link-local, only forgery by a machine on the same link matters.

A forged Query from a lower address makes the forger Querier. If it then stays silent, another router resumes after the Other Querier Present timer runs out, and if the forger ignores Done messages, traffic might flow to addresses without listeners for up to the Multicast Listener Interval. A forged Report may make routers think listeners exist, but listening to a multicast address is generally unprivileged, so a local user can do the same without forging anything. A forged Done only causes extra Queries and cannot cause loss of desired traffic.
sections.eli5: A prankster in the same room can fool the teacher a little, but the worst they can do is cause some extra questions.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Zero from the sender; ignored by receivers.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Standard ICMPv6 checksum over the whole message and a pseudo-header.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero from the sender; ignored by receivers.

fields.name: Multicast Address
fields.desc: Zero in a General Query, otherwise a specific multicast address.

messages.label: General Query to FF02::1
messages.note: Max Response Delay set to the Query Response Interval.

messages.label: Report
messages.note: A's random timer expires first; sent to the reported address.

messages.label: Report heard
messages.note: B stops its timer and sends no Report.

messages.label: Address-Specific Query
messages.note: Sent to the multicast address; if no Report follows, the address is dropped.

items.label: Robustness Variable
items.desc: Tolerates Robustness Variable minus 1 packet losses.

items.label: Query Interval
items.desc: Between General Queries from the Querier.

items.label: Query Response Interval
items.desc: Maximum Response Delay in General Queries.

items.label: Last Listener Query Interval
items.desc: Delay in address-specific Queries after a Done.

items.label: Unsolicited Report Interval
items.desc: Between repeats of a node's initial Report.
